The OBBB claims fiscal responsibility but falls short where it matters. While securing the border and military funding are non-negotiable priorities, the bill’s $1.6T in cuts barely scratch the surface of the $6T needed to reverse Biden-era bloat. Section 3’s Medicaid "strengthening" looks more like padding for pharma middlemen than real reform—block grants tied to drug price transparency would save $200B+ alone.

The rushed 1,100-page drafting process reeks of the same D.C. insider games, with loopholes like SALT cap expansions ($200B/yr revenue loss) undermining deficit claims. Until the Senate strips out special interest carve-outs and replaces “cost-plus” defense contracts with fixed-price models ($150B savings), this isn’t fiscal responsibility—it’s theater.

America deserves actual accountability, not recycled failures.

The One Big Beautiful Bill takes a necessary step by stripping Medicaid from illegal immigrants—taxpayers shouldn’t fund benefits for those breaking our laws. But let’s not pretend this solves systemic waste. The bill’s own projections show it cuts just $1.6 trillion while adding up to $5.8 trillion in new debt.

Real reform would gut the pharmaceutical middlemen skimming $200 billion annually through Medicaid overpayments and end “cost-plus” defense contracts bleeding $150 billion. Instead, D.C. opts for performative cuts while leaving the real graft untouched.

Want lasting change? Pass the Fair Tax Act to incinerate the IRS, eliminate payroll taxes, and force Washington to collect revenue transparently at the point of sale—no more hidden theft from workers’ paychecks. Until then, every “cost-cutting” bill is just rearranging deck chairs on the Titanic.

Fix the structure, not the symptoms.

The Apples to Apples Comparison Act (H.R. 4093) highlights a critical flaw: Medicare's pricing opacity enables systemic waste. While mandating CMS to publish expenditure data by county/MSA is a step forward, the real issue is the 224% premium private insurers pay over Medicare rates for the same services (RAND 2022).

This bill’s Medicare Advantage vs FFS analysis must confront how hospital consolidation distorts pricing—like Lowell General charging $1,677 for a $303 mammogram (KFF 2025). Until CMS enforces strict penalties for non-compliance with transparency rules (current fines are $300/day, less than 1% of average hospital CEO pay), bureaucrats will keep gaming the system.

The solution? Tie Medicare reimbursements to market-driven reference pricing and eliminate facility fee scams that inflate ASC vs hospital outpatient costs.

The numbers don’t lie—see how entrenched interests profit from opacity and what real reform would look like: https://t.co/BL96Hgkgu7

The Florida tax cuts are a textbook example of how state-level reforms can amplify federal fiscal discipline. HB 7031's elimination of the business rent tax—a uniquely Floridian burden that stifled small businesses for decades—is transformative. Combine that with SB 1158's rebate program targeting working families, and you've got a blueprint for economic velocity.

While the "largest tax cut" claim deserves scrutiny (federal H.R.1's $1.6T cuts still hold that crown), Florida's $1.3B relief package smartly pairs permanent sales tax eliminations on essentials with strategic business incentives.

This isn't just about letting families keep more income—it's structural reform to outcompete high-tax states.
